name: Italian Game (Giuoco Pianissimo)
summary: Slow build-up with c3 and d3, then the knight manoeuvre Nb1-d2-f1-g3. Few forced lines, plans that work at every level.

notes.7: c3 prepares d4 later and gives the bishop a retreat on c2. No hurry: the centre stays closed.
notes.9: d3 keeps the e4 pawn solid. The fight is about the d4 square and the f5 square for a knight.
notes.15: Bb3 steps out of ...Na5 and ...d5 tricks before they happen.
notes.19: The knight starts its route d2-f1-g3 (or e3). From g3 it eyes f5; from e3 it covers d5.
notes.23: Ng3: the typical Pianissimo set-up is complete. Plans now: d4 at the right moment, or Nh4-f5 against the king.

notes.7: 4.d3 sidesteps the Fried Liver theory and keeps the same quiet structure as the main line.
notes.13: a4 gains space and stops ...b5; it also gives the bishop the a2 square after ...Na5.
notes.15: Ba2 keeps the strong diagonal towards f7. The knight on a5 will have to come back.
notes.19: Same plan as always: the d2 knight heads for f1 and g3, and d4 comes when it is prepared.

notes.9: Against the bishop on c5 the plan is unchanged: c3, d3, castle, and only then think about d4.
notes.17: h3 takes g4 away from the bishop and knight before Nbd2, so nothing is pinned.
notes.21: Nf1 and Ng3 follow; if Black plays ...Ng6 the e3 route (Nf1-e3) is often better, covering d5 and f5.
